## Methods

Materials
Aluminium (Al, 1~3 μm) with a purity of 99.5% was purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd., China. Titanium (Ti, 100 nm~1 μm) with a purity of 99.5% was purchased from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd., China. Copper oxide (CuO, 20~60 nm) with a purity of 99.5% was purchased from Shanghai Yien Chemical Technology Co., Ltd., China. N-hexane (GC) (purity > 99.5%) was purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagents Co., Ltd., China. Hydroyl-terminated polybutadiene (HTPB) and toluene diisocyanate (TDI) were purchased from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd., China. Ethylacetate (AR) and ethanol (AR) were purchased from Beijing Tong Guang Fine Chemicals Co., Ltd., China. HMX (Type Ⅴ) was obtained from Gansu Yinguang Chemical Industry Group Co., Ltd. All the reagents were used as received without additional purification.

Preparation of ATC–HMX Composite Particles
The “lychee-like” core–shell-structured Al/Ti/CuO MICs (Al:Ti:CuO = 29.89:12.81:57.3 wt%) were first synthesized via a chemical reaction-inhibited ball milling method under mechanochemical forces by following our previously reported protocol46. The as-prepared Al/Ti/CuO MICs were subsequently blended with HMX at four distinct mass ratios (20:80, 30:70, 40:60, and 50:50 wt%) and subjected to acoustic resonance processing (amplitude intensity: 50 g; mixing duration: 20 min). This mixing technique combines macroscopic vibration blending with microscopic acoustic streaming effects through low-frequency, high-acceleration vertical oscillations and yielded four composite formulations: 20ATC–80HMX (20 wt% Al/Ti/CuO + 80 wt% HMX), 30ATC–70HMX, 40ATC–60HMX, and 50ATC–50HMX. A schematic illustration of the preparation process is shown in Fig. 1a. The acoustic resonance was operated at an acceleration of 50 g and a resonance frequency of 62 Hz.

Preparation of ATC–HMX Printing Ink
The ATC–HMX-printed ink was prepared using hydroxyl-terminated polybutadiene (HTPB) as the binder and ethyl acetate as the solvent; the solid content was 88%, with a mass ratio of 40ATC–60HMX powder to HTPB of 88:12. A control HMX sample (HMX:HTPB = 88:12) was also prepared for comparison. For a representative 50 g batch of 88% solid content 40ATC–60HMX/HTPB ink, (10.00±0.01) g of ethyl acetate was first measured into a beaker, followed by the addition of (6.00±0.01) g of HTPB and the curing agent TDI. The mixture was ultrasonically stirred for 10 min to achieve initial homogeneity before incorporating (44.00±0.01) g of 40ATC–60HMX mixed powder and ultrasonic mixing for another 10 min. The ink was then subjected to acoustic resonance mixing at an acceleration of 50 g for 50 min, during which the coupled macrovibration and microacoustic streaming effects transformed the initially disordered particulate system into small spherical aggregates that progressively coalesced into a completely homogeneous ink (Fig. 6a), as schematically illustrated in Fig. 6b, with the final uniform ink sealed for subsequent use in additive manufacturing applications.

3D Printing of ATC-HMX Samples
To regulate the reaction performance and energy release characteristics of the composites through the material macrostructure, the energetic ink was 3D printed using the direct ink writing extrusion system that is shown in Supplementary Fig. 11. Printing was conducted using an Ultimus V Nordson ASYMTEK printer that was equipped with a pneumatic extrusion system. The prepared energetic ink was loaded into a 30 cc syringe and extruded through a nozzle with an inner diameter of 1.3 mm onto a substrate platform. A rectangular printing path of 10 cm × 10 cm was used, with an extrusion pressure of 32 psi and a print speed of 6 mm/s. The printing process is shown in Fig. 7a, and the printed samples are shown in Fig. 7b-h. (In Fig. 7, white represents HMX, and black represents 40ATC–60HMX). The printed samples include “triangular” HMX and 40ATC–60HMX composites, 40ATC–60HMX strands, and cylindrical coaxial “core–shell” structure composites with HMX and 40ATC–60HMX (the cylindrical core–shell structure consists of an HMX core encapsulated by a 40ATC–60HMX shell). The printed samples were then cured in a vacuum oven at 60°C for 72 hours obtain the final formed specimens.

Characterization
Microstructural characterization was performed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, S-4800, Hitachi, Japan) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Tecnai G2 F30, FEI, USA) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS, SuperX, FEI, USA). The phase composition was analysed by X-ray diffraction (XRD, D8 Advance, Bruker, Germany), and the chemical states were determined via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, ESCALAB25R0Xi, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA).

The TG-DSC-FTIR-MS coupled technique was employed to comprehensively analyze the endothermic/exothermic behavior and mass loss/gain of the materials, while simultaneously characterizing the gaseous products, thereby providing a more thorough understanding of their thermal response. In this setup, the TG-DSC analyzer is connected to the mass spectrometer and FTIR spectrometer via capillary quartz tubes for real-time transfer of gaseous decomposition products. During operation, all instruments were started simultaneously by the thermal analysis software, allowing for the synchronous real-time acquisition of thermal, mass, and product evolution signals. To investigate the thermal reaction behavior and decomposition products of the sample, it was analyzed using this coupled TG-DSC-FTIR-MS system (TG-DSC-FTIR-MS Combined System, NETZSCH-STA 449 F3+QMS 403D+ThermoFisher-Nicolet iS50, NETZSCH, Germany, and Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA.) under the following conditions: argon atmosphere, a flow rate of 50 mL/min, a heating rate of 10 K/min, and a sample mass of 3±0.2 mg.

Constant volume combustion tests are usually used to measure the pressure output that is related to energy release68. The increase in pressure is an index of the intensity of combustion and gas expansion and is caused by gas generation and local air thermal expansion during the chemical reaction of energetic materials69. At atmospheric pressure, a powdered sample (200 ± 2 mg) was placed in a quartz crucible and inserted into a constant-volume combustion chamber (fixed volume: 330 mL, Supplementary Fig. 17a). The sample was ignited by a pre-embedded Nichrome wire (Φ 0.03–1.0 mm), which was heated via a DC power supply. The combustion generated a rapid pressure increase and produced a peak pressure (P ) at a specific pressurization rate (P ). The pressure transient was recorded using a ZQ-Y3 pressure sensor (Zhongnan Instrument Co., Ltd., Changsha, China) and a DPO7104 digital oscilloscope (Tektronix Inc., USA). The pressurization rate was determined from the slope of the pressure–time curve between 10% and 90% of P 70. The combustion pressure output test of 3D printed samples in the atmosphere is the same as the above experimental method.

The heat of combustion of the sample was measured using a TRHW-7000C oxygen bomb calorimeter (Hebi Tianrun Electronic Technology Co., Ltd., China) (Supplementary Fig. 17b) under atmospheric pressure; the calorimeter consisted primarily of an oxygen bomb, an insulating jacket, a stirrer, an ignition unit, a temperature measurement and control system, and distilled water. The fundamental principle of the measurement is as follows: The test sample is placed inside the oxygen bomb, which is then immersed in water. Typically, a 200 ± 2 mg sample was placed into a sealed reaction chamber and subsequently ignited using a nickel-chromium wire with a diameter of 0.2 mm under a 5 A current. The heat released from the complete combustion of the sample causes an increase in the water temperature. By recording the initial and final water temperatures, the heat that is required for this temperature change is calculated, which corresponds to the heat of combustion of the sample. For each experiment, a weighed sample was placed in the crucible. A Nichrome wire of a specified length was connected to the ignition electrodes, and the measurement was initiated via program control. Each sample was tested in triplicate, and the average value is reported.

Combustion experiments were conducted in a sealed chamber with multiple viewports under an inert atmosphere, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 18. The chamber consists primarily of observation windows, a shell, a gas inlet, and an exhaust port. The top gas inlet serves as the positive electrode, and the shell acts as the negative electrode. During the experiment, a sample of 200 ± 2 mg was placed in a crucible and positioned inside the visualized sealed combustion chamber (volume: 400 mL). After the chamber was evacuated, it was filled with nitrogen at 0.5 MPa. The sample was ignited by heating an embedded nickel–chromium alloy wire within the powder via a DC power supply that was connected to the positive and negative electrodes (current: 5 A, model: IT-M3144; ITECH Electronics Co., Ltd., Nanjing, China). The combustion process of the sample in the inert atmosphere was recorded using a high-speed camera (model: Revealer X113; Hefei Zhongke Junda Vision Co., Ltd., China).

Flame propagation, which is closely associated with the gas production rate and reaction kinetics, serves as a fundamental parameter for evaluating combustion performance in open systems. A laser ignition experiment was conducted on a powder sample (200±2 mg) using a CO laser (model: K808-25W; Beijing Kaipulin Photoelectric Technology Co., Ltd., China). The flame evolution and temperature change during combustion in an open system were simultaneously recorded by a high-speed camera and an infrared thermal imager, respectively. The spot diameter of the CO laser was 3.0 ± 0.5 mm, with a power of 100 W. Combustion events were captured at 5000 fps using a Revealer X113 high-speed camera, with simultaneous temperature monitoring via an SC300-series infrared imager (FLIR Systems, USA). Ignition delay was defined as the interval between laser initiation and the first visible spark. A schematic diagram of the laser ignition test experimental device is shown in Supplementary Fig. 19.

To investigate the combustion characteristics of HMX and ATC–HMX under oxygen-deficient and weakly confined conditions, we loaded 50 mg of HMX and ATC–HMX powders into quartz glass tubes (as shown in Supplementary Fig. 20) with an inner diameter of 3 mm, a wall thickness of 2 mm, and a length of 5 cm. The tubes were sealed at one end and open at the other end. After natural settling, the powders were ignited at the open end using a CO laser to study their combustion performance under geometric confinement.

To investigate the response behaviour and state of materials under transient high-temperature heating, high-energy laser-induced ignition experiments were conducted on small-scale samples (milligram level)71, 72, with the ignition and shock wave evolution processes recorded using a high-temporal-resolution camera. Schlieren imaging73, a conventional technique for visualizing refractive index gradients along the optical path, was employed to analyse the temporal characteristics of laser-generated plasma and shock waves. The induced dynamics were investigated using a custom laser schlieren system (Supplementary Fig. 21) that consisted of three integrated subsystems: (1) a reaction system that employed a Nd:YAG solid-state laser (Spitlight1000.2-10, InnoLas Laser Company, Germany, with a wavelength of 1064 nm, a maximum energy of 1030 mJ, and a spot diameter of 6 mm) as the energy source; (2) a schlieren imaging system that incorporated a JML-C2 flash background light source (Rapp OptoElectronic, Germany) and an SIMD8 ultrahigh-speed camera (Specialized Imaging, UK) with a minimum exposure time of 5 ns for shockwave visualization; and (3) a control system that comprised a pulse signal generator (Model DG535, Stanford Research Systems, USA) and data acquisition software. Sample preparation involved uniformly depositing 50±2 mg of test material as 0.5±0.1 mm thick layers on 12 mm diameter stainless steel moulds using double-sided adhesive, with complete coverage of the circular mould surface ensured.

The rheological behaviour of the printed slurries was characterized using a rotational rheometer (MCR 72, Anton Paar, Austria). Measurements were conducted at 25°C with a 1 mm gap. Shear rate sweeps were performed in logarithmic mode from 0.1 to 100 s-1 to evaluate the shear-dependent viscosity profile. Additionally, amplitude sweeps were carried out at a fixed frequency of 10 rad/s with a strain that varied logarithmically between 0.01% and 100% to investigate the strain-dependent viscoelastic properties, including the storage modulus (G') and loss modulus (G'').

The densities of the printed samples were measured using an MDJ-120TEM densimeter (Shanghai Yixin Scientific Instrument Co., Ltd., China). In accordance with GJB 772A (Explosives test methods, China), standard impact, friction, and electrostatic discharge sensitivity tests were conducted on the printed composite systems.

To investigate the detonation performance of 3D-printed HMX+ATC–HMX “core–shell” composite charge samples (the cylindrical “core–shell” structure of HMX+ATC–HMX consists of an HMX core that is encapsulated by a 40ATC–60HMX shell), air blast experiments were conducted in an explosion chamber according to the setup that is shown in Supplementary Fig. 22. The sample dimensions were Φ30 × 40 mm. The free-field overpressure from the sample explosion was measured using a model 137B22 shock wave pressure sensor (PCB Piezotronics, USA). The signal was then conditioned by a model 483C signal conditioner (PCB Piezotronics, USA) and subsequently acquired by an NI PXIe-5162 high-speed data acquisition module (National Instruments, USA), with the system sampling rate set at 1 GHz. A high-speed camera (SH6-116, Shenzhen SinceVision Technology Co., Ltd.; frame rate: 40,000 fps) and a high-temperature infrared imager (MAG-F7(E), Shanghai Magnity Technologies Co., Ltd.; frame rate: 131 fps) were used to record and monitor the detonation process of the sample. Simultaneously, two monitoring cameras inside the explosion chamber were used to observe the overall macroscopic reaction of the samples. Composite witness plates that were composed of 2A12 duralumin and cotton were used to assess the effects of the blast diameter and macroscopic damage at distances of 50 cm, 75 cm, 100 cm, 125 cm, and 150 cm from the sample. The sample platform was positioned 1.5 m above the ground. Two overpressure measurement lines were arranged approximately 90° relative to each other. Each line contained two pressure sensors as measurement points, which were located 33 cm and 66 cm from the sample centre. The sensors were positioned at the same height as the charge in the same horizontal plane. An electric detonator was used to initiate the samples.

The theoretical thermodynamic parameters of the samples were calculated using the REAL-WIN thermodynamic program (version 3.0, evolved from an earlier ASTRA program), which simulates real experimental conditions. Under constant-volume and adiabatic conditions (V = 1.65 m3·kg-1, H = 0 kJ·kg-1), the volume of a closed bomb (330 mL) was input. Assuming no energy exchange with the surroundings, all energy released from the reaction was converted into a temperature rise of the system. The heated gaseous products expanded, exerting pressure on the vessel, thereby allowing the calculation of the combustion temperature (T, K) and pressure (P, kPa) at reaction equilibrium. Under constant-volume and isothermal conditions (V = 1.65 m3·kg-1, T = 298.15 K), the heat of combustion (Q, kJ·kg-1) and the mass fraction of condensed products (Mcond) at equilibrium were computed. Under constant-pressure and adiabatic conditions (P = 0.1 MPa, H = 0 kJ·kg-1), the energy released caused the gaseous products to expand, and the specific volume of the gas phase (Vg, m3·kg-1) at equilibrium was determined. Based on these three sets of conditions, the relevant thermodynamic parameters for the ATC-HMX system were calculated.

At first glance, the paper accumulates too much information without sufficient in-depth investigation regarding the mutual interaction mechanisms at either slow solid state thermal analysis or fast burning to declaration under laser shock. The major driving force and chemical pathways are not clear in all reactions. As a scientific paper, the merit of this formulation design should be persuasive, but this paper seems like an experimental report without sufficient instructive insights to the readers.

Secondly, the reported DIW technology herein is not the advanced one, which uses only HTPB-TDI curing system. It largely depends on the solid loading of the compositions. If the solid loading is too high, there might be flow problems and otherwise the curing time is too long to be well shaped to obtain the desired charge structure. The defects herein must be a lot, and the bulk density should be far below the theoretical maximum density. Therefore, the detonation velocity and pressure cannot be higher than normal cured formulations with the same ingredients. Therefore, BET and density parameters could be measured and compared with normal cured ones.

In case of flame propagation, the rate greater than 900 m/s cannot be called as “shockwaves”; The explosive with thermobaric effects must have lower overpressure than normal explosives with less metal contents. The formulations of HPTB/RDX-88/12 may reach overpressure of 300 kPa at 2 m location.

The research is suggested to be focused on the reactivity and energy release mechanisms of the new formulations without HTPB, since there are no extra findings on DIW technology. The reaction mechanisms might be clarified without HTPB binder, which is too complicated to be well described. There is no concept of “acoustic resonance-assisted integration and direct ink writing”, since these two steps are separated. If the acoustic mixing is online, that would be much better.

The particle size distributions are the major issues for the manufacturing processes. It must be well studied if the authors focused on DIW technology.

The burning process must be measured in presence of N2 or Ar, better with pressure. The compositions of the condensed products must be measured. CEA calculations can be done for optimized formulations if HTPB is included. The thermal decomposition behavior was dominantly determined by the content of HMX, which generates most of the gaseous products. Therefore, if possible, in presence of different metals, the decomposition kinetics and mechanisms might be changed. As physical mixtures, the XRD and IR spectra of the MICs products are not important to present.

The English is not promising. There are a log of grammar errors and terminology problems, such as “Lines” should be “strands”. The revised paper is suggested to be submitted to CNF and PCI as more specified journals.

### Reviewer 4

The submitted manuscripts by Ren and colleagues describe an unprecedented integration of the synthesis of energetic Metastable Intermolecular Composites (MICs) by the RAM technique and further 3D-printing. Although there is enough literature precedents about energetic MICs, the novelty of this work is highlighted by the unique methodology of synthesis and the corresponding enhancement of properties of these MICs. The authors have investigated all the relevant properties related to energetic MICs, ranging from combustion studies, detonation studies, rheological properties, and many more. The ATC additive lowers the decomposition temperature of HMX and enhances its energy output significantly. The authors also elaborately investigated the mechanisms of the interaction between ATC and HMX using the REAL software. The manuscript can be accepted for publication in Nature Communications after a minor revision considering the following points:

1. Although the body and volume of the work done are huge, the length of the manuscript seems a bit stretched. The authors can think of summarizing significant findings using tables, figures, graphs, etc.
2. Direct Ink Writing (DIW) of energetic composites is well explored in references 42-49. The novelty of the present work, as compared to these prior arts, should be explained clearly. Specifically, the advantages offered by the present 3D-printing methodology should be emphasized.
3. Is it possible to provide experimental evidence regarding the advantages offered by RAM mixing as compared to traditional ball-milling? A performance comparison with the ATC-HMX composite prepared by conventional methods can be helpful.
4. Did the authors test the impact, friction, and electrostatic discharge sensitivity of the 3D-printed composites?
5. The authors should provide detailed information regarding the 3D printing, including nozzle diameter, pressure, speed of writing, etc. (Please see Section 2.4 in reference 45).
6. Can the authors explain why the filaments show ‘secondary pressurizations’ while core-shell prints give a fireball?
7. Why did the authors only consider HMX for their MICs? MICs with CL-20 are also known, and CL-20 often gives better energy output, although it is more sensitive.
8. The performance of the present ATC-HMX composite should be compared with other related MICs and presented in a tabular form. (For eg. Al/Ti/CuO-B MICs previously reported by the authors)
9. In the conclusion section, the authors claim that 3D printed ATC-HMX composites have a superior density to HMX. However, no numerical values are mentioned to justify this claim.
